format: 20 minutes each: 15-minute talk plus 5-minute discussion; 12 main slides and 2 optional backups

conceptual.title:
When is a collective
an agent?
conceptual.subtitle:
Predictive organization and
responses to changed rules
conceptual.notes: 45 seconds. The question is when we gain explanatory power by treating a collection as an agent. There are three connected issues: agency in general, collective agency, and human agency within a collective. This talk focuses on the second. The companion talk asks about human control. We now have a stronger starting point than a chain of related ideas: Hammond and coauthors already formalize collective agency using causal abstraction. I want to ask what predictive organization adds to that framework, and what comparison could show that it adds nothing. This is a research proposal with a checked illustration, not a completed empirical result. The cover is a conceptual illustration, not data.

conceptual.title: The question to investigate
conceptual.statement: When does an agent model predict collective responses better than a predictive pattern does?
conceptual.body: Fix the boundary, goals, and interventions before comparing models.
conceptual.notes: 75 seconds. Consider a team whose routine decisions are easy to forecast. That forecast alone does not tell us how the team will react to a new incentive, a changed communication rule, or a member challenging the objective. A collective-agent model should explain some of these responses through a relatively economical account of goals and adaptation. The proposed comparison asks whether a macrodescription selected for predictive compression also works for these interventions. We should restrict the goals and intervention maps before evaluating outcomes; otherwise we can fit a story to almost anything. The point is to compare explanations on the same systems, with held-out changes.

conceptual.title: Different claims need different evidence
rows: Macro history suffices for a specified future.
Regulation sustains the system’s own organization.
conceptual.caption: Rosas et al. 2024; Kenton et al. 2022; Barandiaran et al. 2009; List & Pettit 2006
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. These are not rungs of one agreed definition. Computational mechanics studies predictive organization. Kenton and colleagues focus on policies adapting when the consequences of actions change. Barandiaran, Di Paolo, and Rohde ask for autonomous organization and norms grounded in it. List and Pettit emphasize robust rational representational and goal states in group agents. A reward-maximizing controller can fit a behavioral account without demonstrating endogenous norms. A group can satisfy a rationality model while members have little influence. Our main operational comparison uses behavioral agency and explicitly leaves the stronger autonomy and institutional questions open. Ask the group which account they want the model to explain.

conceptual.title: What closure and blankets give us
items: Closure
Does the macro past retain the micro past’s predictive information?
Causal blanket
Which directional statistics summarize exchange across a chosen split?
Boundary choice
Compare candidates; blanket existence does not pick an agent.
conceptual.caption: Rosas et al., Software in the natural world; Causal blankets. Bruineberg et al. 2022.
conceptual.notes: 75 seconds. Predictive causal states group histories by their future distributions. Informational closure asks whether knowing the micro past adds anything to predicting the macro future once the macro past is known. That can make a macrodescription scientifically useful. It does not establish an unrestricted intervention result, and a constant macrovariable passes trivially. Causal blankets identify minimal directional statistics for a chosen system–environment split. They are available for each bipartition, so existence alone does not identify the right agent. Bruineberg and colleagues give a related conceptual caution about treating statistical blankets as worldly boundaries. This is a caution about interpretation, not a refutation of the causal-blanket construction.

conceptual.title: From a stream to a world model
items: Fixed-policy prediction
What happens while the current behavior continues?
Controlled interface
What would be observed under another allowed action?
Mechanism response
How do participants revise policies when the rules change?
conceptual.caption: Rosas, Boyd & Baltieri, AI in a vat; Hammond et al., Reasoning about causality in games.
conceptual.notes: 75 seconds. AI in a vat gives us the action-conditioned bridge. Instead of only predicting a stream, a world model represents observations under possible action sequences. This is already established work and should not be presented as our innovation. It still fixes a controlled generator. In an organization, a rule change can cause participants to change the policies they use. Hammond and colleagues distinguish interventions with policies held fixed from interventions known when policies are selected. The distinction is about the information available to policy selection, not simply whether an event happens early or late. We need to include that mechanism response in what the proposed macro model predicts.

conceptual.title: Collective agency already has a formal model
items: Alignment
Say which micro variables and interventions represent each macro variable.
Consistency
Mapped micro outcomes agree with macro outcomes under those interventions.
Agency claim
A restricted goal-and-response model explains the macro behavior.
conceptual.caption: Jørgensen, Weichwald & Hammond 2026, Definitions 8–15; actor–critic and voting examples.
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. Causal Foundations of Collective Agency is the closest prior work. It formalizes mechanized abstraction: map micro variables to macro variables, map interventions, and require agreement of the induced outcome distributions. The framework can have multiple equilibria, hence sets of distributions rather than one prediction. It then asks whether the macro mechanism behaves rationally relative to a utility and rationality relation. The paper proves an actor–critic example and gives a voting application. Those are existing contributions. Our narrower proposed comparison concerns the relation between predictive compression and this strategic abstraction. We have not established that the comparison is novel across the whole literature.

conceptual.title: Same baseline, different response
conceptual.caption: Checked illustration: Y = 1 XOR A XOR g; adaptive A = g; frozen A = 0.
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. This tiny example is useful because it separates an observation from an interpretation. Let g indicate whether actuation is reversed and let the desired outcome be one. Under ordinary actuation, both systems choose zero and reach the target. When reversal is announced, the adaptive system chooses one while the frozen system stays at zero. Their baseline behavior is identical, but the mechanism response differs. The calculation is checked by exact enumeration. It is not new agency theory, and a simple conditional controller can realize the adaptive behavior. That is why conventional adaptive control belongs among our baselines. The example is a diagnostic, not evidence of collective or autonomous agency.

conceptual.title: What the feedback paper establishes
items: Formal result
A product prior stays factored under the specified feedback update.
Reported neural evidence
Synthetic transformers often represent and use those factors; some edits fail.
Further question
Does a represented factor also support a goal-and-response explanation?
conceptual.caption: Ehrlich, Baltieri, Rosas & Boyd 2026, arXiv:2611.02047v1. No replication here.
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. The public feedback paper is now identified correctly, with David Ehrlich, Manuel Baltieri, Fernando Rosas, and Alexander Boyd as authors. The factorization proof preserves a product belief under a particular delayed feedback construction. It does not say arbitrary correlated priors become products. Masking an exchanged token requires summing product operators, which need not remain a product. In synthetic transformers the authors report factor decoding and successful belief edits, with failures in some sns-containing settings. These results help explain a predictor’s computation. They do not by themselves identify internal goal-directed agents. We should test that extra claim instead of assuming the terminology settles it.

conceptual.title: A comparison we can actually run
rows: Does compression transfer to changed mechanisms?
Does a restricted utility explain strategic responses?
Does ordinary mechanism modeling explain just as much?
conceptual.caption: Proposed benchmark: matched data and stated computation budgets; not yet run.
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. Start small, with known coupled controllers. Include an actor–critic positive control, a frozen or replay negative control, and adaptive-control baselines. Choose candidate boundaries and outcomes first. Train or identify models on a limited intervention family, then test on held-out mechanisms and observation masks. Report error together with representation and computation costs, since a large unrestricted model can absorb many behaviors. We should not declare a collective agent solely because it fits the training data or because the microdescription is cumbersome. For equilibrium models, compare sets or specify a selection rule. This benchmark is proposed; we have not implemented the experimental comparison.

conceptual.title: What would weaken the agency interpretation?
items: No added economy
An adaptive component model predicts just as well at comparable cost.
Goal overfitting
The macro utility must be refitted after every intervention.
Boundary instability
The preferred unit changes with small, irrelevant modeling choices.
conceptual.caption: MacDermott et al. 2024 offers a goal-directedness comparator; utility/model choices remain explicit.
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. The main hypothesis is that predictive compression and strategic explanatory value can rank boundaries differently. We also need to be willing to find that the agent model adds little. If a conventional adaptive model predicts equally well at comparable cost, that limits the explanatory gain from agency language. If the utility has to be rewritten after every test, the model has not generalized. A very flexible utility class can rationalize behavior without predicting much; maximum-entropy goal-directedness is a useful comparator but still depends on causal and utility choices. Boundary sensitivity can also reveal that our conclusion is an artifact of the representation. These outcomes are informative research results, not failures to tell an attractive story.

conceptual.title: The contribution is still a proposal
conceptual.statement: Test the relationship between predictive compression and strategic explanatory value.
conceptual.body:
The collective-agency framework already exists.
The cross-model comparison remains to be done.
conceptual.notes: 90 seconds. We now have a specific comparison rather than a historical narrative. The literature supplies definitions and examples. Our executed contribution so far is limited to elementary diagnostic calculations. The proposed contribution would be a controlled benchmark identifying when a compressed predictive description remains useful for strategic interventions, when it fails, and whether an agent model improves explanation. It may turn out that existing adaptive-control or abstraction methods already answer the task. Further novelty review is needed. Even a successful synthetic benchmark would not establish autonomy in living systems, institutional legitimacy, or human control. Those require additional evidence and, for authority, explicit normative commitments.

conceptual.title: Discussion
conceptual.statement: What must an agent model explain that a predictive model does not?
items: Interventions
Which changed rules should the model survive?
Baseline
What would count as no added explanatory value?
Boundary
Do learning and institutional rules belong inside the agent?
conceptual.notes: 300 seconds. Use the remaining five minutes for these three questions. Start with a concrete collective the group cares about and specify one intervention whose outcome matters. Then identify a plausible non-agentic or conventional control explanation. Ask whether the learning process is inside the modeled boundary; Kenton’s account makes that consequential. If the group prefers an autonomous or institutional account, identify what extra observations would be required. End by choosing one tractable comparison, rather than agreeing only that all the papers connect.

conceptual.title: Backup: three cautions
items: Predictive closure
Relative to chosen variables and futures; a constant macro can pass.
Mechanized abstraction
Depends on alignments, admissible interventions, and solution concepts.
Belief dimension
Distribution parameters and PCA ranks are not universal neural or human limits.
conceptual.caption: Source definitions and qualifications are developed step by step in the mathematical companion.
conceptual.notes: Optional backup. Use this slide if the discussion slips from one notion of closure to another. Predictive informational closure is not the same as biological closure of maintained constraints. Mechanized abstraction preserves specified intervention semantics; it does not certify every conceivable intervention. A factorized distribution has a compact parameterization, but minimal reachable belief dimension and neural encoding dimension are different questions. None of these mathematical properties alone supplies a measure of a person’s practical authority.

organizational.title:
What must people
retain control over?
organizational.subtitle:
AI islands, useful summaries,
and the ability to correct decisions
organizational.notes: 45 seconds. The first talk asked when a collective deserves an agent model. This one asks whether people can direct that collective. A group can become effective at pursuing an objective while its members become less able to question or change it. Alec’s AI-islands proposal gives us a concrete design to investigate. I will make the workflow explicit, use Lauffer’s minimal-knowledge result to clarify what reports must preserve, and separate the information problem from decision rights. The numbers in the worked example are invented and checked analytically. The organizational pilot remains a proposal.

organizational.title: The core question
organizational.statement: What must survive a handoff for a person to make a warranted correction?
organizational.body: Relevant information and effective decision rights must be evaluated separately.
organizational.notes: 75 seconds. The goal is not for everyone to reconstruct every internal interaction. It is for the right people to have evidence that can change a decision and a usable way to act on it. We need to specify whose reasons count, which decisions can be revisited, and how much time there is before execution. More information can overwhelm someone; less information can hide exactly the fact that matters. A simple summary can be sufficient for one objective and fail after an authorized objective change. This gives us a specific research question rather than a general claim that transparency or human review is always good.

organizational.title: A concrete islands workflow
items: Local work
Each person and assistant develops a resource-allocation proposal.
Reviewed handoff
Evidence, assumptions, uncertainty, and dissent travel with the proposal.
Correction
People can query, revise, refuse, or appeal before execution.
organizational.caption: Our operationalization of the supplied XOR Labs / Alec proposal; fictional task, no pilot run.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. Imagine a resource-allocation exercise with several teams. Each assistant can inspect local evidence and suggest a plan. A cross-team handoff carries not just a recommendation but its assumptions, evidence references, uncertainty, and any disagreement. A person reviews and forwards it, can request underlying evidence, and can refuse a proposed action. Final decision and execution permissions are specified separately, with an appeal route for affected people. These workflow details are our operationalization of the supplied AI-islands idea. They should not all be attributed to Alec. The important question is which part of the design creates any benefit: mediation, evidence access, or actual rights to change the outcome.

organizational.title: Do not bundle four different changes
rows: Hide messages or summarize the same transcript.
Remove a channel or introduce review delays.
Give someone an enforceable pause or revision.
organizational.caption: Hiding a channel from an observer does not simulate deleting it from the system.
organizational.notes: 75 seconds. This separation is the backbone of the study. Masking a message changes what someone can observe. Removing the message channel changes the interacting process. Giving someone a veto changes available actions. Changing the criterion for a good allocation changes the objective. An islands design can change all four at once, making its apparent benefit difficult to explain. First use a fixed generator to isolate the information effect. Then compare live communication arrangements with matched final rights and evidence access. Finally vary rights independently. Some interactions will remain, but stating them explicitly is much better than attributing every improvement to human mediation.

organizational.title: Who needs to know what?
items: Existing result
Co-policies are strategically equivalent when they induce the same best-response set.
Useful compression
Keep distinctions that change the decision; other details can be omitted.
Scope
Equivalence depends on the decision problem, including objectives and feasible actions.
organizational.caption: Lauffer, Shah, Carroll, Dennis & Russell (ICML 2023), Who Needs to Know?
organizational.notes: 75 seconds. Lauffer and coauthors give us a precise starting point. For one player, take the other participants’ possible policies and group those that induce the same entire set of best responses. Those classes retain the distinctions needed to recover that set. This is stronger than merely retaining one common optimal action. Their computational work focuses on common-payoff dynamic games, while the paper states that the theory extends to general-sum settings. We should not pretend this is a new result. Our question is how a reporting interface performs when an authorized decision context changes, and whether a human can actually infer and use the reported distinctions.

organizational.title: A summary can fail after priorities change
organizational.caption: Checked toy example: routine report merges C and E. Revised objective needs to distinguish them.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. Here the co-policy can be C, D, or E, each equally likely. Under the routine objective, A is best in C and E, so one report can merge those types. Under the revised objective, E instead calls for B while C still calls for A. The old report has erased a relevant distinction. The companion gives the complete payoff table: under the revised objective, A pays four, zero, zero across C, D, E, while B pays two, three, two. With full information the expected value is three. With the old C/E report, both actions average two in that cell, giving total value seven thirds. The information loss is two thirds.

organizational.title: Less required knowledge can mean less control
organizational.caption: Invented unitless payoffs; uniform prior. Exact enumeration, not a human-subject result.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. Now remove the right to choose B. The only feasible best response is A for all types, so no information is needed to recover it. The information regret relative to full information under those same restricted rights is zero. Nevertheless, attainable value has fallen to four thirds. This shows why minimal information alone is an inadequate measure of control. One must compare both information loss within a rights arrangement and the options available across rights arrangements. The script exhausts every deterministic partition of the three types and checks the arithmetic exactly. It establishes this illustration, not a general effect size for organizational oversight.

organizational.title: What the world-model work contributes
items: Feedback prediction
Masking exchanged tokens can break a useful factorization.
Strategic response
Announced rule changes can alter other participants’ policies.
Human control
A compact predictor does not settle whose reasons guide execution.
organizational.caption: Ehrlich et al. 2026; Rosas et al., AI in a vat; Hammond et al. 2023; Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven 2018.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. The feedback paper gives a reason to worry about hiding interactions: the observer’s belief may become harder to represent. It does not prove that exposing every interaction helps a person make a decision. AI in a vat helps distinguish prediction from action-conditioned modeling. Hammond and colleagues further show why an announced rule change differs from a surprise event with policies fixed. Finally, Santoni de Sio and van den Hoven emphasize responsiveness to relevant human reasons and tracing to people with understanding and responsibility. A click on an approval screen is evidence of neither by itself. These literatures constrain the design in different ways; none alone establishes the best workflow.

organizational.title: Compare three designs
rows: Direct assistant exchanges with evidence and provenance.
A person reviews and forwards each handoff.
Routine exchange; review on specified conflicts.
organizational.caption: Proposed comparison: match final correction rights, task resources, model version, and evidence access.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. These three designs allow us to ask whether universal mediation adds something beyond evidence access and targeted escalation. Keep final correction rights comparable at first. Introduce routine cases, errors, cross-team inconsistencies, and an explicitly authorized change in priorities. For a replay experiment, freeze the generator and compare reports. For live interaction, allow the design to affect delay and strategic adaptation, and measure those effects. A report can be refreshed after a context changes if evidence and time remain available; this is a serious alternative to requiring every future-relevant distinction in the initial handoff. We should compare fixed and adaptive reporting rather than make the compressed baseline artificially weak.

organizational.title: Measure correction, cost, and influence
items: Correction
Did evidence change the decision before execution? Whose objection mattered?
Cost
Regret, false interventions, delay, and workload.
Rival explanation
Logged collaboration with escalation may work as well or better.
organizational.caption: No organizational experiment run. Numerical thresholds and sample planning remain to be specified.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. Correction success is central, but it should not be measured without costs. A workflow can stop errors by stopping useful work too. Record false interventions, delay, workload, and whether source evidence was actually accessible. Also report whose objections change outcomes and who can revise the objective. Where stakeholders disagree, do not silently combine them into one team payoff. The rival hypothesis is that direct logged collaboration with selective escalation provides the same correction capacity more cheaply. If so, the general case for universal islands weakens. We have not justified numerical success thresholds or a sample size; the toy values are not empirical estimates for power analysis.

organizational.title: A conditional organizational implication
organizational.statement: Preserve the distinctions needed for correction—and the rights to act on them.
organizational.body:
Test mediation against alternatives.
Collective capability does not establish member control.
organizational.notes: 90 seconds. The recommendation we can currently defend is to specify what people must be able to challenge, preserve access to evidence that could change those judgments, and test whether their interventions really affect execution. Human mediation may be useful when it exposes omitted evidence and prompts effective challenge. It can fail through rubber-stamping, lack of expertise, bottlenecks, or corrupted handoffs. Separate channels can still share model errors and incentives. If a benefit comes entirely from an enforceable veto, that supports the veto rather than universal message review. Our task is to identify those mechanisms and the conditions under which they work.

organizational.title: Discussion
organizational.statement: What must an affected person be able to notice, challenge, and change?
items: Objectives
Who can authorize a change in priorities?
Evidence
Which distinctions must survive, or remain retrievable?
Test
What outcome would count against universal mediation?
organizational.notes: 300 seconds. Reserve five minutes for these questions. Ask the group to pick a concrete allocation or coordination decision. Identify the affected people and which reasons should count, rather than assuming a single manager is the only relevant human. Then specify one correction that the workflow must permit and the evidence needed to justify it. Finally ask what result would lead us to prefer logged collaboration or selective escalation instead of islands. This should produce a bounded pilot question and an explicit authority assumption, not a general endorsement of human oversight.

organizational.title: Backup: complete payoff table
organizational.caption: All types have probability 1/3. Source: repository-authored verify_strategic_reports.py.
organizational.notes: Optional backup. The routine partition is C/E versus D. The revised partition is C versus D/E. Their common refinement has three singleton cells. With a fixed report serving both contexts, all three types must be distinguished to recover the full best-response set. This is an elementary common-refinement construction based on Lauffer’s SER, not a new theorem. For another task, preserving one common optimal action can need fewer distinctions than recovering the entire set; the companion gives an overlapping-set example.
